text: Coccidiosis mainly affects calves 1–6 months old. Signs: appetite/weight loss and general wasting; profuse diarrhea that can contain blood and mucus; straining during defecation (abdominal pain); in milder, more common cases, dull/broken hair and poor condition, with diarrhea turning blackish and mucous-like, sometimes forming a compact lump stuck around the tail. Treatment: Sulfa 33 for 5 days. E. coli diarrhea in newborn calves: picked up while suckling or through the umbilical cord, appearing in the first days after calving. Signs: yellow-white diarrhea, the calf becomes very weak and stops nursing, and infection can spread to the umbilicus, joints, or become general septicemia. Treatment: take a diarrheic newborn calf off milk immediately; if severely dehydrated (sunken eyes), give IV fluid or, if unavailable, an oral electrolyte solution — plain water alone doesn't work. A simple homemade version: 3 big spoons of sugar and ½ big spoon of salt dissolved in 2 liters of mild (lukewarm) water, given at 1 liter every 6 hours. Dehydrated calves often also have low body temperature and need to be kept warm, especially at night. Inject antibiotics too: Colistin or TMP+Sulfa. Prevention: calves are born with no E. coli antibodies of their own and depend entirely on colostrum (available only for a few hours after birth) for protection, so ensuring good colostrum intake within the first 12 hours of life is crucial.
